rv.q: Daldry often gives it the heart-pounding tension of a thriller, with memorable scenes like a night-time Soviet raid and a perilous train journey.
Lan’s play burns with care about the casualties of horror and the dogged determination of those trying to do something good in the face of unspeakable evil.
Stephen Daldry ensures that his production is never less than an audio-visual feast...
It’s a blast of theatricality and a triumph of intellect which has obvious lessons for our times, even if they sometimes drown out the heart.

If the occasionally baggy drama doesn’t quite justify a running time of nearly three hours, it’s held together by an imperious performance by Juliet Stevenson as Ruth, a UN relief worker in the shattered landscape of postwar Germany.
Yet the pace is too slow (almost three hours) and the characters around Ruth are generic, from the classically cocky Yanks to the oh-so-British aid workers.
The Land of the Living is sprawling, uneven, and occasionally frustrating.
And yet the conundrum of The Land of the Living is that, for all its pedigree, something essential and affecting never quite materialises.
Gripping, poignant and, at times, chilling - put it on your ‘must watch’ list.
But the direction cannot disguise the fact that the play is too long, circling back on its arguments, and becoming over-extended and flat in the process.
The action tends to come in jolts, with long scenes often jarred by sudden action or violence.

Quite why he wouldn’t have preferred to remain with his new-found siblings and delve deeply into their past, rather than make a transatlantic flight, appears to be a moot point in David Lan’s undoubtedly well-meaning and heavily researched play.

cn.t: Lan's humane drama about Nazi-abducted children earns praise for Stevenson's powerhouse performance and Buether's stunning design, but critics find the sprawling play uneven and overlong, struggling to match its ambitious moral questions with dramatic impact.
